Uri Aloni, son of Aviva and Avraham, was born in Jerusalem on the 28th of Kislev 5736 (2 December 1975). He was the younger brother of Roni and Sharit, and the older brother of Shir.

Uri studied at the Gershon Agron elementary school and the David Ston elementary school in Jerusalem. He continued his studies at the ORT Beverly Minkoff middle school and completed his secondary education at the ORT college in Givat Ram.

Uri was curious and wide-ranging. He read hundreds of books in Hebrew and English and was especially fond of science fiction. He wrote poems and short stories, one of them a book he never finished, and several of his poems were published in the school newsletter. He also wrote scenarios for Dungeons & Dragons games for a group of friends who played together for many years. He loved computer games, had a wide knowledge of technology, and was once interviewed on the educational television program in its morning show. When he finished high school he received a prize for community service. When he was fourteen, his parents divorced.

Uri was drafted into the IDF in mid-January 1994 and assigned to the Logistics Corps. After basic training, and after completing a quartermaster course, he was sent to the north, to the Golan Heights and Lebanon. After seven months he was transferred to Neve Yaakov in Jerusalem to serve at a Logistics Corps base. Because of family difficulties, the IDF recognized him as a lone soldier.

Private Uri Aloni fell during his service on the 17th of Elul 5754 (24 August 1994), at the age of nineteen. He was laid to rest in the military cemetery on Mount Herzl.

In a letter of condolence to the bereaved family, Chief of Staff Ehud Barak wrote: "Uri, of blessed memory, was a Logistics NCO in an emergency supply unit. His commanders described him as a serious, disciplined and quiet soldier." His commander wrote: "Uri was a quiet, friendly and orderly soldier, notable for his seriousness."

At the initiative of his sister Sharit, the family commemorated his name in the Kiryat HaYovel neighborhood. They donated fifty science fiction books to the Philip Lahav Community Center library and set up a corner dedicated entirely to the genre he loved. They bought learning equipment for pupils at the Gershon Agron elementary school, where he studied in his early years. They donated his textbooks to the ORT college where he studied and set up a memorial corner in the biology laboratory, his favorite subject. Additional books were donated to the high school affiliated with the university.

In his memory, a book was published collecting his work, "Shirat HaEinsof" (The Poetry of Infinity), and it is available at bit.ly/urialoni.

His sister Shir directed a documentary film about his story and his works. The film took part in the Women Filmmakers Festival at the Cinematheque in Tel Aviv, and it can be viewed on YouTube under the title "HaSof" (The End).
